# Polytopes

Polyhedra as topology first and coordinates second. An abstract incidence complex you can build and validate; the Conway operator algebra — `dual`, `ambo`, `kis`, `truncate`, `gyro` and the composites written over them — that rewrites it, with per-element provenance and lineage carried through every step; and three realization verbs that hand the result coordinates: `realize` for a first embedding, `relax` for one that satisfies constraints you declare, and `canonicalize` for the classical edge-tangent form you would recognise as a solid. Everything is immutable and CPU-only; `FieldAdapters.kt` is where a polytope becomes `FLine`s or a `TriMesh`. 4-polytopes, their Schlegel and slice projections, and an OFF importer live here too. Files are listed alphabetically below; a reader new to the package wants `Topology.kt`, then `Transforms.kt`, then `Conway.kt`, then `Canonical.kt`, then `FieldAdapters.kt` — and [Polytopes: topology first, coordinates later](../polytope_examples.md) for the same ground with pictures.

## Attributes.kt { #attributes-kt }

Untyped per-element data, carried alongside the topology and propagated through transforms.

An attribute is how a caller writes something onto one vertex, edge or face and gets it back later:
a per-face height for a non-uniform `kis`, a colour that survives into the FLine and triangle
output, a tag a selector can test with `ElementSelectors.attributeEquals`. What crosses a Conway
operator is decided by an [`AttributePropagationPolicy`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-attributepropagationpolicy) rather than by each operator, and the
default — [`PreserveCommonAttributes`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-preservecommonattributes) — keeps only the entries every source element agreed on.

Values are typed `Any?`: these are Field's ordinary property values, so a box can put an
`Int`, a `Vec3` or a lambda in one. Two consequences follow: equality is
structural `==` on `Any?`, so `1` and `1.0` are different attributes, and nothing here validates a
value against a schema. The two extension functions `PolyhedralObject.withAttribute` and
`PolyhedralObject.withAttributes` are the intended entry points, because unlike
[`PolytopeAttributes`](polytopes.md#attributes-kt-polytopeattributes) itself they check that the element exists.

## Canonical.kt { #canonical-kt }

Canonicalization: the step that turns combinatorially-correct-but-lumpy Conway output into the
solid you were picturing.

A polyhedron's **canonical form** is the embedding in which every edge is tangent to one common
sphere, the centroid of those tangency points is the origin, and every face is planar. For a convex
polyhedron it exists, and — up to Möbius transformations of the sphere, which the origin-centring
fixes — it is unique. It is also determined by the *combinatorics alone*, which is the fact that
makes this file useful: the coordinates you hand in are only a starting guess, so
`canonicalConway("gD")` and a hand-built pentagonal hexecontahedron converge to the same solid.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val solid = canonicalConway("bkD").polyhedron        // notation straight to geometry
val result = cube().ambo().polyhedron.canonicalize() // or repair an embedding you already have
```

### The two iterations

`CanonicalMethod.RECIPROCAL` alternates polar reciprocation between primal and dual and reaches the
fixed point in tens of steps, but requires every face plane to stay away from the origin.
`CanonicalMethod.LOCAL_RELAXATION` takes small bounded local steps — tangency, recentring,
planarity — and is slow but robust. The default runs the first and polishes with the second. When an
attempt fails, `CanonicalizeOptions.reseed` restarts from coordinates built from the topology alone;
`CanonicalizeResult.reseeded` always says whether that happened.

### Read the diagnostics

`CanonicalizeResult.converged` means the iteration stopped moving, and no more than that.
[`CanonicalDiagnostics`](polytopes.md#canonical-kt-canonicaldiagnostics) is the evidence, reported before and after, and a run that ends with
a large `tangencyRadiusSpread` has failed and says so. The floor on all of it is about `1e-7`
relative, because [`Realization3`](polytopes.md#solids-kt-realization3) stores single-precision coordinates.

## CeresRealization.kt { #ceresrealization-kt }

Optional bridge: run a [`RelaxationPlan`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-relaxationplan) on the native Ceres solver instead of the built-in one.

### It needs the native library

Everything in this file requires the `ken-ceres` wrapper to be built and loaded — there is no
pure-Kotlin path here, and nothing is committed. Build it once with
`./gradlew buildCeresRedistributable`; see `dev_docs/CERES.md`.
`ceresRealizationAvailable` answers whether this JVM has one, and `PolyhedralObject.relaxWithCeres`
throws a description of what is missing rather than falling back to `PolyhedralObject.relax`, so a
result reported as Ceres's was solved by Ceres.

### What it buys

The same objective, solved properly. `PolyhedralObject.relax` takes a central finite-difference
Jacobian and forms a dense `3V x 3V` normal matrix every iteration; Ceres differentiates each
residual analytically over only the parameters it touches and can factor the sparse normal equations,
so the per-iteration cost tracks the number of *incidences* rather than the square of the vertex
count. On `kkC` and `kkD` that decides whether there is an answer at all: both reach a tangency
spread of `1e-8` in 12 iterations and about 6 ms, where `relax` takes 1507 ms and does not converge.
Plus a real termination report in [`CeresSolveSummary`](solvers.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceressolvesummary).

A second implementation of the same declared objective, running alongside the built-in one:
same plan in, the same [`RealizationSolveResult`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-realizationsolveresult) out, the same [`RigidGauge`](polytopes.md#realize-kt-rigidgauge) applied afterwards, so the
two can be run on one plan and diffed. Three places where they genuinely differ — the plane
parameterisation, the weight convention and the robust loss — are set out on [`CeresRealization`](polytopes.md#ceresrealization-kt-ceresrealization), and
the fourth is `CeresRelaxationOptions.minEdgeLengthFraction`, which guards a defect in the objective
that both solvers share.

Not everything crosses over. `CeresRealization.unsupported` names the families with no native
equivalent; in practice that means a custom [`RealizationConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-realizationconstraint) or [`SymmetryOrbitConstraint`](polytopes.md#symmetry-kt-symmetryorbitconstraint), so
`RelaxationPlan.Companion.symmetricCanonical` cannot be solved here.

## Constraints.kt { #constraints-kt }

The constraint vocabulary a realization run is written in.

A [`RealizationConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-realizationconstraint) is one named, immutable family of residuals — "every edge the same
length", "every face planar", "the tangency centroid at the origin". A [`RelaxationPlan`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-relaxationplan) is a list
of them, so a realization run is *data*: it prints, it diffs, it reweights with
`RelaxationPlan.withWeight`, and it can be handed to a second minimiser and the answers compared.
[`RealizationProblem`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-realizationproblem) is the boundary that makes that cheap: it derives the edge endpoints, the face
cycles and the initial coordinates once per solve, and hands a constraint nothing but flat
`DoubleArray` coordinates and integer indices — no [`ElementId`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-elementid) bookkeeping, no FLines, no renderer.

### Units, and what a weight multiplies

Every residual in this file is a **length in the units of the coordinates**, and every one is
written as `weight * (measured - goal)`. So the families are directly comparable to each other, and
a weight is a plain multiplier that enters the least-squares cost as its square.

What a weight is *not* is a share of influence, because the families contribute very different
numbers of residuals for the same object:

- [`EdgeLengthConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-edgelengthconstraint) and [`EdgeTangencyConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-edgetangencyconstraint) — one per edge.
- [`CommonRadiusConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-commonradiusconstraint) — one per vertex.
- [`FacePlanarityConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-faceplanarityconstraint) — one per face **corner**, so it is usually the largest block.
- [`ProximityConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-proximityconstraint) — three per vertex.
- [`CentroidConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-centroidconstraint) and [`TangencyCentroidConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-tangencycentroidconstraint) — three, whatever the object's size.

On a cube: 12 edge-length residuals, 8 common-radius, 24 face-planarity, 24 proximity, and 3 for
either centring family. The default blends in `RelaxationPlan.regularize` and
`RelaxationPlan.canonicalConditions` give the three-residual centring families a much larger weight
for exactly this reason; read a weight as calibration against a residual count, not as a priority.

### Reporting

`RealizationConstraint.residualCount` may not depend on the coordinates, which is what makes a run's
residual vector sliceable per family after the fact. `report` goes one step further and re-evaluates
each family at weight 1, so a [`RealizationSolveResult`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-realizationsolveresult) can state each family's error in the units of
the thing constrained rather than in solver units.

### Writing your own

Implement the interface: it is four small members and nothing in this file is privileged. Two rules
that are not obvious — write exactly `RealizationConstraint.residualCount` entries starting at the
offset you are given, and make `withWeight(1.0)` genuinely unweighted, since that is what `report`
relies on. A custom family has no Ceres equivalent, so a plan containing one cannot cross over to
`PolyhedralObject.relaxWithCeres`; `CeresRealization.unsupported` names it.

## Conway.kt { #conway-kt }

Conway prefix notation: the one-line string that names a polyhedron by how it is built.

`conway("bkC")` reads right to left — start from the cube, kis it, bevel that — and hands back a
[`PolytopeTransformResult`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-polytopetransformresult) with the full lineage attached. That is the whole public surface most
callers need. `parseConwayExpression` exposes the parse on its own, for a UI that wants to report a
bad character's offset before running anything, and `canonicalConway` is the same evaluation
followed by a canonical embedding.

### The notation this accepts

A final seed letter — `T C O I D` for the five Platonic solids — preceded by any number of the
operator letters in [`ConwayOperator`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-conwayoperator). Whitespace is ignored anywhere. Two operators additionally
accept a **degree selector** written as digits after the letter: `k5D` kises only the pentagonal
faces, `t3C` truncates only the degree-3 vertices. That is a Field extension of the notation, built
on [`ElementSelectors`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementselectors); digits after any other operator are a parse error rather than a silent
ignore, and so is a digit with no operator to attach to.

### What it will not do

There is no grouping, no repetition count and no seed beyond the five Platonics — no `(ka)3T`, no
prisms, no antiprisms. Coordinates come from each operator's default realization policy, so a long
expression evaluates to something combinatorially exact and geometrically drifted; reach for
`canonicalConway` when you want a solid you would recognise.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Conway.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Conway/)

## FieldAdapters.kt { #fieldadapters-kt }

The bridge from a polytope to the things Field can actually draw: `FLine`s and a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

Three adapters, and the choice between them is about what you want to *do* with the result rather
than how it looks. `PolyhedralObject.toFaceFLines` gives one closed line per face, which is what
you want if faces are going to be styled, picked or filled independently. `PolyhedralObject.triangulate`
gives a flat-normal [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) with the provenance arrays needed to get from a triangle or a render
vertex back to the element it came from; `PolyhedralObject.toTriMesh` is the same thing when that
provenance can be thrown away. `Polytope4.toEdgeFLines` projects a 4-polytope to a wireframe.

### Attributes become FLine properties

Every face line receives its face's attributes copied straight into `line.properties`, plus
`POLYTOPE_FACE_ID_PROPERTY` and `POLYTOPE_FACE_RANK_PROPERTY`. So an attribute named `color` set
on a face during a Conway chain arrives as Field's own `color` property with no translation step —
which is the point of [`PolytopeAttributes`](polytopes.md#attributes-kt-polytopeattributes) being typed as `Any`, and also means a badly-named
attribute can overwrite a drawing property with no warning.

### What these will not do

Every entry point requires a realization and validates the topology first, so an abstract polytope
throws rather than drawing nothing. A face with zero area throws [`DegenerateFaceGeometryException`](polytopes.md#fieldadapters-kt-degeneratefacegeometryexception)
rather than emitting a triangle with a garbage normal.

### Faces with holes

A face's inner rings (`topology.faceHoles`) travel the whole way through both adapters.
`PolyhedralObject.triangulate` hands them to a [`HoleAwareFaceTriangulator`](polytopes.md#fieldadapters-kt-holeawarefacetriangulator) — the default
[`EarcutFaceTriangulator`](polytopes.md#fieldadapters-kt-earcutfacetriangulator) is one — and a face with holes given a triangulator that is *not*
hole-aware throws rather than filling the hole in. `PolyhedralObject.toFaceFLines` emits each hole
as a further closed contour on the same `FLine`, which is exactly what `FLine.tessellate` and
`PlanarTessellation` already understand, so a filled holed face fills with a hole in it and a
stroked one is drawn with its inner outline.

Holes change nothing about a face that has none: positions, indices, normals and both provenance
arrays match the hole-unaware triangulation exactly, over the five Platonic seeds, `bC` and a
windowed cube with its ring dropped (`PolytopeFaceHolesTest`).

`PolyhedralObject.faceNormal` reads the outer ring only: a hole does not contribute area, and its
opposite winding would cancel some of the outline's if it did.

### Flat, smooth, or creased

[`NormalPolicy`](polytopes.md#fieldadapters-kt-normalpolicy) decides what normal each duplicated corner carries. The default is `NormalPolicy.Flat`
— one face normal per face, which is what a Conway solid wants, every edge of one being a real
crease. `NormalPolicy.Crease` averages the faces at a vertex that are within an angle of this one,
so a subdivided sphere reads as curved and a cube still reads as a cube. Nothing else about the
output changes: same vertices, same triangles, same provenance arrays.

## Off.kt { #off-kt }

The one-way bridge to OFF, the plain-text polygon interchange format that Geomview and most
polyhedron tooling read.

One function and no reader. Export exists so that a solid can be opened in something
that was not written here — an independent second opinion when a test disagrees with a picture — and
so that a bug report can carry the actual object. Nothing else in this package goes through it,
and no part of the topology is shaped by what OFF can express.

The format itself is lossy for this library's purposes. Element identity, rank structure above 2,
attributes and provenance all disappear; what survives is coordinates and polygons.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Off.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Off/)

## Parameters.kt { #parameters-kt }

Naming a subset of elements, and attaching a number to each one.

This is the small algebra that turns a Conway operator from a whole-object rewrite into something
applied *there, by that much*. [`ElementSelector`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementselector) says which elements take part;
[`ElementDoubleParameter`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementdoubleparameter) says how much, for each of them independently. The selective `kis`,
`truncate` and `gyro` overloads take both, evaluate them once per candidate element, and record
what they resolved in a [`TransformDeployment`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-transformdeployment) — so a non-uniform operation stays inspectable and
replayable after the fact rather than being a number you typed once.

### Evaluating a selector

Both interfaces are single-method predicates over an [`ElementSelectionContext`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementselectioncontext): the object, one
element, and that element's lineage when there is one. They are called once per candidate element,
in `topology.elements(rank)` order, with no caching and no batching — so keep them cheap and free
of side effects.

The **operator chooses the rank, not the selector.** `kis(selector, …)` offers the selector only
`elements(2)`, `truncate(selector, …)` only `elements(0)`, and `gyro` takes no selector at all and
evaluates its parameter over every edge. `ElementSelectors.rank` therefore filters *within* the
operator's rank rather than redirecting it: `kis(ElementSelectors.rank(0))` matches nothing and
kis-es nothing, legally and silently.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
// Raise an apex over the pentagons only, by an amount painted onto each face beforehand.
val result = solid.kis(ElementSelectors.faceDegree(5), ElementParameters.attribute("spike"))
```

### Lineage is not always there

`ElementSelectors.provenanceRole` is the one selector that needs transform history.
`PolyhedralObject.selectElements` builds a context without lineage, so on a bare object every
provenance test is false — and a *negated* provenance test is therefore vacuously true, which is
the standing trap in this file. Ask a [`PolytopeTransformResult`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-polytopetransformresult) when a role matters.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Parameters.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Parameters/)

**Used in:** [Polytopes: topology first, coordinates later](../polytope_examples.md)

## Polytope4.kt { #polytope4-kt }

Rank 4: the seeds, the coordinates and the viewing policy that exercise the incidence core at a
rank a polyhedron library never reaches.

Four regular seeds — `fiveCell`, `tesseract`, `sixteenCell` and the self-dual `twentyFourCell` —
plus [`Realization4`](polytopes.md#polytope4-kt-realization4) for coordinates, an abstract `Polytope4.dual`, and [`Projection4`](polytopes.md#polytope4-kt-projection4) for getting a
picture out. Everything a rank-3 reader would assume is wrong here: there are four
proper ranks rather than three, an edge bounds three or more polygons rather than exactly two (so
`validate(checkManifold = true)` *must reject* a tesseract, and does), and there is no
`triangulate()`, because a projected 4-polytope's polygons do not bound a surface and filling them
would claim they did.

### Deriving the face lattice

`convexPolytope4` is the one call the seeds are built from. You give it vertex coordinates and
outward facet normals; it works out cells, polygons, boundary orders and edges itself. So a wrong
derivation shows up as a wrong published count — 24 cells, 96 edges — rather than as a shape nobody
checked. The trade is in the name: the criteria it uses are true of convex polytopes and only of
convex polytopes.

### Coordinates are `DoubleArray`

Field's graphics vocabulary has no `Vec4` and should not grow one for this, so [`Realization4`](polytopes.md#polytope4-kt-realization4)
stores plain `DoubleArray`s and every public read hands back a copy. That also means rank 4 is the
double-precision half of this package while `Realization3` is single-precision.

### Projection is a camera, not geometry

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = tesseract()
val points = t.project(RotatedProjection4(0, 3, angle = 0.6))   // cube inside a cube, turning
```

A [`Projection4`](polytopes.md#polytope4-kt-projection4) lives *above* realization: swapping one for another changes the picture and not
the object, and nothing in the topology moves when you do it.

## PolytopeVisualizers.kt { #polytopevisualizers-kt }

The single place this package knows that Field has a screen — and it is one function long.

Each printer registered here reduces its value to one of the plain summary data classes in
`Summaries.kt` — `PolytopeTopologySummary`, `Polytope4Summary`, and so on — and hands *that* to
Field's ordinary reflective value visualizer. So a topology, a transform result or a
canonicalization plan left as a box's last expression prints something useful, while nothing in
the topology depends on `FLine`, meshes or a renderer, and `println(x.summary())` shows the same
facts because it is the same value.

## RealizationSolver.kt { #realizationsolver-kt }

The middle realization verb: improve an embedding you already have.

`realize(policy)` builds coordinates for a topology that has none, `PolyhedralObject.canonicalize`
seeks the symmetry-respecting representative, and `PolyhedralObject.relax` — this file — takes an
embedding and a declared set of constraints and moves the vertices until the constraints are as
satisfied as a local descent can make them. A run is a [`RelaxationPlan`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-relaxationplan): a list of named
[`RealizationConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-realizationconstraint) values, an [`afield.stdlib.LeastSquaresOptions`](math.md#leastsquares-kt-leastsquaresoptions), and an optional
[`RigidGauge`](polytopes.md#realize-kt-rigidgauge). The answer is a [`RealizationSolveResult`](polytopes.md#realizationsolver-kt-realizationsolveresult) carrying every family's *unweighted*
geometric error before and after, so the reader can see which constraint gave way rather than only
how small the blended cost got.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val result = cube().relax(RelaxationPlan.regularize())
result.finalConstraints.forEach { println("${it.name}  rms ${it.rms}  max ${it.max}") }
```

### What is minimised

`afield.stdlib.leastSquares` runs Levenberg-Marquardt on half the squared norm of every active
family's residuals concatenated. A weight is a plain multiplier on its family's residuals, so it
enters the cost as its *square*; and because families contribute wildly different residual counts
— three for a centroid, one per face corner for planarity — equal weights are not equal influence.
See `Constraints.kt` for the counts.

The iteration is local and descent-only. It stops at a stationary point of that one sum and claims
nothing about a global minimum, uniqueness, convexity, or the absence of self-intersection;
`RealizationSolveResult.converged` means a tolerance was met, not that the answer is the one you
wanted. Where the objective itself has a degenerate minimum — the canonical conditions do, because
a collapsed edge satisfies [`EdgeTangencyConstraint`](polytopes.md#constraints-kt-edgetangencyconstraint) for free — a converged run can be nonsense, and
only the diagnostics will say so.

### Cost per iteration

The Jacobian is central finite differences, so an iteration costs `2 * 3 * vertexCount` residual
evaluations and builds a dense `3V x 3V` normal matrix. That is the right tool for exact control
over tens of vertices. For hundreds use `PolyhedralObject.canonicalize`; to hand the same declared
plan to a sparse second-order solver, `CeresRealization.kt` — which needs a native library.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/RealizationSolver.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/RealizationSolver/)

## Realize.kt { #realize-kt }

Coordinates from combinatorics alone, and the gauge that makes an answer a *representative*.

Two unrelated jobs, kept in one file because the second is what makes the first reproducible.

`PolytopeTopology.realize` is the first of the library's three realization verbs. It differs from
[`RealizationPolicy3`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-realizationpolicy3), which computes a Conway output's coordinates from its *source's*: a
[`RealizationConstruction`](polytopes.md#realize-kt-realizationconstruction) sees only the incidence structure and must invent an embedding from
nothing. [`SpectralRealization`](polytopes.md#realize-kt-spectralrealization) is the one built in — the low Laplacian modes of the vertex graph,
which is exactly the symmetric solid for a vertex-transitive graph and a good symmetry-respecting
starting point otherwise.

[`RigidGauge`](polytopes.md#realize-kt-rigidgauge) is the other half. Every constraint family in this package is invariant under rigid
motion, and most under scale, so a solver's answer is only defined up to seven degrees of freedom.
Leaving that to a weak proximity term makes results depend on solver damping; instead
`PolyhedralObject.normalize` translates a declared centre to the origin, scales a declared measured
length to a target, and — given a reference embedding — applies the one rotation that best matches
it. The rotation gauge is anchored to a reference rather than to the inertia tensor, because the
principal axes of a symmetric solid are degenerate, so an inertia gauge would spin.

A construction can return a self-intersecting embedding with
non-planar faces and this file will not notice; that is what `PolyhedralObject.canonicalDiagnostics`
and `PolyhedralObject.geometryDiagnostics` are for.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Realize.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Realize/)

**Used in:** [Polytopes: topology first, coordinates later](../polytope_examples.md)

## Solids.kt { #solids-kt }

The rank-3 value everything in this package passes around, and the five Platonic seeds to start
from.

[`PolyhedralObject`](polytopes.md#solids-kt-polyhedralobject) is the aggregate — a [`PolytopeTopology`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-polytopetopology), optional coordinates, optional
per-element attributes — and [`Realization3`](polytopes.md#solids-kt-realization3) is the coordinate half, kept as a separate immutable
value so that a Conway operator can replace it wholesale without the topology noticing. The seeds
are `tetrahedron`, `cube`, `octahedron`, `icosahedron` and `dodecahedron`; each returns a fully
realized, outward-wound, manifold-validated object, and each is the starting point of a Conway
expression such as `conway("tI")`.

`cubeWithWindow` is the sixth and the odd one out: a cube whose top face has a hole in it, which
makes it a surface *with boundary* rather than a closed manifold. It exists so that the parts of
the library that handle holes have something real to be tested and demonstrated against.

### Scale is not uniform across the seeds

`tetrahedron`, `octahedron`, `icosahedron` and `dodecahedron` all put their vertices on the unit
sphere. `cube` does not: it is the ±1 cube, so its side is 2 and its circumradius `sqrt(3)`. If you
are comparing seeds, or mixing them in one scene, normalise or apply a gauge first rather than
assuming a common radius.

### Seed faces are wound outward

Seed faces are declared as unoriented index cycles and then reversed where needed so that every
normal points away from the vertex centroid. Which means the literal lists below need only be
correct as *cycles* — a reader checking them does not also have to check their handedness.

## Summaries.kt { #summaries-kt }

Small, plain data classes that reduce the library's big values to something printable.

The mathematical types in this package contain no HTML and know nothing about presentation.
`PolytopeVisualizers.kt` registers a value printer for each big type
that reduces it to one of these summaries and hands *that* to Field's ordinary reflective
visualizer. So a bare `polyhedron` or `result` as a box's last expression is informative, and the
same facts are available programmatically — `println(result.summary())` reports exactly what the
inspector shows, because it is the same call.

### What to trust in them

They are lossy, and a few of the losses matter:

- **A summary is a *snapshot*, not a view.** Every one of these is computed eagerly from the value
  at the moment you ask, and several are not cheap: `PolytopeTopology.summary` runs the validator,
  twice for a valid rank-3 topology.
- **Counts of things are exact; the *identity* of things is gone.** [`PolytopeTopologySummary`](polytopes.md#summaries-kt-polytopetopologysummary)
  reports how many faces have each degree but not which; [`SymmetryDeviation`](polytopes.md#symmetry-kt-symmetrydeviation) reports the worst
  spread but not the class it came from. Go back to the underlying value for that.
- **A `null` almost always means "not measurable" rather than "no".**
  `PolytopeTopologySummary.closedManifold` is null when the check was not run, and
  [`Realization3Summary`](polytopes.md#summaries-kt-realization3summary)'s bounds are null for an empty realization.
- **Names are used as keys, so same-named things collapse.** `RelaxationPlanSummary.weights` is
  keyed by constraint family name and [`PolytopeTransformSummary`](polytopes.md#summaries-kt-polytopetransformsummary) lists operator display names, so
  two edge-length families with different targets, or two distinct operators printing the same
  name, are indistinguishable in the summary.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Summaries.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Summaries/)

## Symmetry.kt { #symmetry-kt }

Symmetry as a combinatorial fact, and as something a solver can be asked for.

The library never computes a symmetry *group*. It computes a partition — `combinatorialOrbits` —
of the elements into classes that no automorphism of the topology can tell apart, by iterated
incidence-colour refinement over the ranked incidence structure. Coordinates play no part, so the
classes of a lumpy embedding and of its canonical form are identical: they are a property of the
combinatorics.

Two things are built on that. [`SymmetryOrbitConstraint`](polytopes.md#symmetry-kt-symmetryorbitconstraint) turns the partition into residuals — same
edge length within an edge class, same vertex radius within a vertex class, same face-plane distance
within a face class — so a realization run can be *asked* to look symmetric, and
`RelaxationPlan.Companion.symmetricCanonical` is the canonical conditions plus that family.
`symmetryDeviation` is the readout in the other direction: how equal the geometry actually is inside
each class, as a relative spread.

### The caveat that runs through all of it

Colour refinement is not a complete isomorphism invariant, so a class is a *union* of true
automorphism orbits and may be strictly coarser than them. Constraining a class is therefore at
least as strong as constraining an orbit — and on a topology where it is strictly stronger, the
constraint asks for an equality no embedding can deliver. That case is not detected: the
`symmetry-orbit` family reports a real residual and the reader is expected to look. The
long-term fix named in `dev_docs/POLYTOPE_ALGEBRA.md` is Wythoff construction, which would supply
actual group orbits.

These are all soft constraints. Nothing in this file projects onto a symmetry group's fixed
subspace, so nothing here can manufacture symmetry the topology does not have.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/polytope/Symmetry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/polytope/Symmetry/)

**Used in:** [Polytopes: topology first, coordinates later](../polytope_examples.md)

## Topology.kt { #topology-kt }

The abstract incidence complex — the authoritative value in `afield.stdlib.polytope`, and the one
layer that knows nothing about coordinates.

A [`PolytopeTopology`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-polytopetopology) is a set of ranked [`Element`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-element)s with identity, incidences between *adjacent*
ranks only, and an explicitly ordered vertex boundary per rank-2 face. Nothing in this file holds a
position, an `FLine`, a triangle, a normal or a renderer; a `Realization3` sits above it and can
be replaced or thrown away without disturbing the combinatorics. That separation is what lets a
Conway operator discard every coordinate, make new ones, and still answer "which face is this,
and what was it before".

Ordered cycles are stored rather than derived because unoriented incidence does not choose a
traversal: four edges in a ring are equally consistent with two different quadrilaterals. A cycle
*can* be recovered from incidence where a boundary happens to be a single ring —
`PolytopeTopology.dual` does that for its own output — but that is a construction step, not a
property of the poset.

### Ranks, and the element that is the whole thing

Ranks are zero-based: 0 vertices, 1 edges, 2 polygons, 3 cells. A topology's
`PolytopeTopology.rank` is its *top* rank, and by convention the element or elements there stand
for the whole object rather than for a geometric feature. So a polyhedron is rank 3 with one
rank-3 element meaning "the solid", and its proper ranks are `0 until rank`. This is why
`PolytopeTopology.eulerCharacteristic` sums the proper ranks only: it returns 2 for a closed
polyhedral surface and 0 for a convex 4-polytope, which are the numbers a reader is checking
against.

### Validation reports; it does not throw

[`PolytopeTopologyBuilder`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-polytopetopologybuilder) records what it is told and checks almost nothing. Structural
complaints are [`ValidationIssue`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-validationissue) *values* returned by `PolytopeTopology.validate`, so a tool or a
test can see everything wrong with a malformed input at once, rather than the first thing. Call
`ValidationResult.throwIfInvalid` — or `PolytopeTopologyBuilder.buildValidated` — where an
exception is what you actually wanted.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val b = PolytopeTopologyBuilder(rank = 3)
val v = List(3) { b.addElement(0) }
val f = b.addElement(2)
b.setFaceCycle(f, v)
b.build().validate().issues.forEach { println(it.message) }   // three edges never recorded
```

### Faces with holes

A face's boundary is an outer cycle plus zero or more *inner* cycles — see [`FaceBoundary`](polytopes.md#topology-kt-faceboundary).
`faceCycle` returns the outer ring, which is what the twenty-odd callers of it in this package
mean. A hole belongs to its face rather than being a rank-2 element in its own right, so it
carries no attributes and no picking id, and casts no vote in `eulerCharacteristic`;
`cellularEulerCharacteristic` is the reading that subtracts one per hole.
`dev_docs/POLYTOPE_ALGEBRA.md` weighs that shape against the alternatives.

**Winding is a convention here, not a check.** Outer rings run counter-clockwise about the face
normal and inner rings run clockwise. There are no coordinates at this layer, so that cannot be
verified here — and nothing downstream depends on it either, because
`afield.graphics.PlanarTessellation` normalises each ring's winding and decides which ring is the
outer one geometrically. What `validate` does check is combinatorial: rings vertex-disjoint, each
ring closed over the face's own edges, every incident edge used by exactly one ring, and one
boundary component per ring.

A holed face is a surface *with boundary* — its hole edges bound one face, not two — so
`validate(checkManifold = true)` rejects it, correctly. `dual` and the Conway operators require a
closed manifold and therefore refuse it explicitly, rather than dropping the hole silently.

### What is absent

No orientation of the complex as a whole, and no assumption that it is a closed manifold:
`validate(checkManifold = true)` is an opt-in stricter pass, and a 4-polytope legitimately fails
it because an edge there bounds three or more polygons. No incidence between non-adjacent ranks.
And no general incidence-poset isomorphism — `isCombinatoriallyIsomorphicTo` is a rank-3 helper
and says so.

## Transforms.kt { #transforms-kt }

The Conway operator algebra: thirteen named operations that rewrite a polyhedron's combinatorics,
each paired with a policy for giving the result coordinates.

A transform happens in two independent halves, and keeping them apart is the whole point of this
file. `PolytopeTopology.transform` is pure combinatorics — it consumes an incidence complex and
produces a new one plus, for every output element, an [`ImmediateElementProvenance`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-immediateelementprovenance) naming the
source elements it came from and the role it plays (`face-center`, `edge-midpoint`,
`kis-triangle`, `gyro-pentagon`, …). A [`RealizationPolicy3`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-realizationpolicy3) then reads those roles and computes
coordinates from the source's; an [`AttributePropagationPolicy`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-attributepropagationpolicy) does the same for attributes. Swap
the policy and you get a different solid over identical combinatorics.

### Five primitives, eight composites

`d` dual, `a` ambo, `k` kis, `t` truncate and `g` gyro are implemented. `j n z o e s m b` are
defined as primitive *words* — `j = da`, `b = ta`, `s = dgd`, `o = jj`, `m = kj` — and run one
primitive at a time, so they cost as many topology rebuilds as their expansion is long.
`PolytopeTransformResult.history` is the expanded trace; `notationHistory` keeps the composite you
actually asked for.

### Beyond standard notation

`k`, `t` and `g` also take an [`ElementSelector`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementselector) and an [`ElementDoubleParameter`](polytopes.md#parameters-kt-elementdoubleparameter), so one step can
kis only the pentagons, or truncate every vertex by a fraction that varies with its height. Conway
notation cannot say either thing; [`TransformDeployment`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-transformdeployment) records what was selected and which
scalars were resolved, so such a step is still exactly replayable.

### Every operator is on both receivers

All thirteen are declared on [`PolyhedralObject`](polytopes.md#solids-kt-polyhedralobject) *and* on [`PolytopeTransformResult`](polytopes.md#transforms-kt-polytopetransformresult), so a chain
reads the same wherever a step sits: `cube().ambo().bevel().kis()`. The composites take no
realization policy in either position, which is the runtime rule from `transform` expressed in the
signature instead.

### What this will not do

- **Rank 3 and closed manifolds only.** Every step validates its input *and* its output with
  manifold checking on, so a non-manifold complex or an inconsistently oriented vertex fan throws
  rather than producing a plausible-looking bad mesh. A face with a hole is refused by name: it is
  a surface with boundary, and the operators are not defined on one.
- **Nothing here produces a canonical shape.** The default policies are cheap local constructions —
  a centroid, a midpoint, a fraction along an edge — so a long chain drifts away from anything
  symmetric. `PolyhedralObject.canonicalize` is the repair.
